paras: People’s suggestibility varies hugely, both between individuals and according to state, whether you’re talking about external or internal suggestion, and the type of suggestion (commands, imagery, music, metaphors, spiritual etc). There are definitely advantages to both working with someone and doing it yourself, and it depends on what you’re trying to do. A professional can bring pacing, containment and another set of eyes, and doing it yourself gives you instant follow-up, real-time correction and a private line to your own protectors.

paras: Finding a hypnotist who can work with you

Things to ask: What are they trained to treat? How do they use hypnosis in their practice? What will they do if something doesn’t “fit”? If you are working with trauma: Did they actually get training in trauma and dissociation in addition to whatever hypnosis certification they might have? (Remember, credentials matter, but they don’t guarantee competent care!)

fixes.what: credentials matter without guaranteeing competent care
fixes.replace: (Remember, credentials are not indicators of quality care!)
fixes.with: (Remember, credentials matter, but they don’t guarantee competent care!)

fixes.what: what they are trained to treat
fixes.replace: What do they train in?
fixes.with: What are they trained to treat?

paras: Tell them what has and hasn’t worked for you in the past. How direct you want them to be. What kind of touch (if any) you are ok with. What kind of imagery (if any) you are ok with. What to do if you want to stop a session. And ask them what they do about unexpected reactions in or after a session, about things you aren’t sure are memories, and how they do the full return at the end. Keep in mind that a good person should be able to firmly encourage you without making it continue if you say you don’t want to.

fixes.what: the list is what to tell them (describe), not questions
fixes.replace: What has and hasn’t worked for you in the past.
fixes.with: Tell them what has and hasn’t worked for you in the past.

fixes.what: the full return, not 'coming back to the session'
fixes.replace: What to do if you need to come back “all the way” to the session.
fixes.with: How they do the full return at the end.

fixes.what: you tell them what helped, your directness, touch, imagery and how you'll stop; you ask about unexpected reactions, uncertain memories and the full return
fixes.replace: What to do if you have unexpected reactions in or after a session. What to do if you aren’t sure if something is a memory or not. How they do the full return at the end.
fixes.with: And ask them what they do about unexpected reactions in or after a session, about things you aren’t sure are memories, and how they do the full return at the end.

paras: Afterwards, look at what actually happened, not the method’s name. Why they used it (if they said). Whether or not you agreed to it. How the person responded to you (again, keep in mind that discomfort doesn’t mean it was “bad,” but seeing your objections as meaning you needed more of the same might be worth looking into). You can ask the app or others knowledgeable about dissociation and trauma to help explain what happened, but it is unlikely someone can tell you if the person was “certified” or not just based on what you tell them. Depending on what you find out, you might want to try self-hypnosis, combining the two, or finding another practitioner. Those stay your choices.

paras: When the subconscious speaks like an oracle

The subconscious can notice things the conscious mind misses. Anticipations, pattern reads, or just things that seem a bit uncanny that come from it should be respected. The subconscious may send out the image of something or tell you to do something, but that does n't mean it is an order.

fixes.with: should be respected, but not just obeyed, because

paras: If it is something big, or can not be undone easily, it needs to be slowed down to the scale of its consequences, looked at with the adult’s questions, and brought to a council.

fixes.with: slowed down to the scale of its consequences, looked at with the adult’s questions, and brought to a council.

paras: The council — internal first, then outward

First go within; ask the child in you, the adult in you, the conscious and subconscious minds, your intuition and analysis. But if the thing is larger than any of those, go outside for more help. The bigger and more irreversible the move, the more you need to look outside.

Go to people who love you, people who are like you, or people who have traveled that path. Of course sometimes going alone is the right thing, but I would do that as a last step, after first seeking counsel.
On the other hand, it is possible to give your power away. Seeking counsel can quietly turn into abdicating to an authority figure. Another person doesn’t get automatic trust, or automatic dismissal.

fixes.what: neither automatic trust nor automatic dismissal
fixes.replace: It doesn’t mean either trusting or not trusting someone.
fixes.with: Another person doesn’t get automatic trust, or automatic dismissal.

fixes.what: seeking counsel can quietly turn into obeying an authority (a warning, not a definition)
fixes.replace: Seeking counsel doesn’t mean abdicating to an authority figure.
fixes.with: Seeking counsel can quietly turn into abdicating to an authority figure.

paras: Sometimes you need the support of your peers. In Hearthwork, the concept is that you give each other equal time, warmth, confidentiality, and acceptance of “no” as an answer, and you act for each other as Nurturer and Protector, but not as Guide. Then you reverse roles. Sometimes, with a question asked carefully and at the right time, your peers can help you hear your own Guide more clearly, but they don’t interpret what you experience.

fixes.with: with a question asked carefully and at the right time, your peers can help

paras: Forgiveness without bypass

We can’t “force” forgiveness, it has to come from a place of understanding, otherwise it becomes a bypass. And yet staying angry forever can let the injury keep running the present. How do we hold all of this? It can all be true together: the harm happened, the boundary still matters, the person is still accountable, and forgiveness may come later, when your relationship to what happened changes on its own.

fixes.what: a heading-like prefix
fixes.replace: Some Thoughts on Forgiveness: We can’t
fixes.with: We can’t

fixes.what: staying angry forever lets the injury keep governing the present; what can all be true together
fixes.replace: And yet, sometimes it’s also not so great to stay in anger forever. How do we hold all of this? It can all be true.
fixes.with: And yet staying angry forever can let the injury keep running the present. How do we hold all of this? It can all be true together: the harm happened, the boundary still matters, the person is still accountable, and forgiveness may come later, when your relationship to what happened changes on its own.

paras: A helpful understanding to come to, is that while their actions were harmful, in a sense, they could only make the moves they made, given their accumulated nature at the time (conditioning, history, pain, capacity, etc). This doesn’t negate that harm was caused, holding someone accountable, allowing for consequences, working on making different moves now, etc. It simply helps us come to a place where we aren’t expecting something from someone that they can’t give. It doesn’t make their limitations matter any less.

fixes.replace: while their actions may have been harmful,
fixes.with: while their actions were harmful,

fixes.what: understanding limitations shouldn't make them less consequential
fixes.replace: that they can’t give.
fixes.with: that they can’t give. It doesn’t make their limitations matter any less.

paras: “You don’t have to forgive before you’re ready. I won’t use spirituality to silence your pain. And I won’t build our whole life around this wound forever.”

paras: Some questions that may be helpful to ask when coming to a place of forgiveness, while still holding all of the above:

What actually happened? What was the impact? What boundaries need to be set? What shaped the other person(s) into someone capable of that harm? What is theirs? What is mine? What does accountability require? How can I let this go, without denying any of the above?

fixes.replace: What was going on with the other person(s) that put them in a place to cause harm?
fixes.with: What shaped the other person(s) into someone capable of that harm?

fixes.replace: How do I need to hold them accountable?
fixes.with: What does accountability require?

paras: For self-forgiveness, name what you did, without taking responsibility for what wasn't yours. Let the remorse register the harm, or how it went against your values, without making yourself a permanent criminal.

Take responsibility, feel the remorse, then rectify if you can, and then let it go. Be specific about the action you took, and the impact it had, feel the remorse, do what you can to rectify or keep it from happening again, and then stop holding yourself hostage.
